title: Applications of Sets in Survey and Word Problems

blocks.text: Imagine you are conducting a survey in a market to find out how many people buy rice, beans, or both. How can you organize this information efficiently?

blocks.markdown: Sets are a powerful tool to solve problems involving groups of items or people. In this lesson, we will learn how to handle survey data using set theory, particularly focusing on two and three overlapping groups.

blocks.title: Key Formulae
blocks.text: For two sets, $n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)$. For three sets, we use $n(A \cup B \cup C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - n(A \cap B) - n(B \cap C) - n(A \cap C) + n(A \cap B \cap C)$.

blocks.markdown: Let's explore how these formulae are applied in solving problems involving two and three sets. We will also learn to interpret terms like 'only A' and 'neither' in exam questions.

blocks.title: Two-Set Problem
blocks.prompt: In a survey of 100 people, 60 like jollof rice, 45 like fried rice, and 25 like both. How many people like either jollof rice or fried rice?

steps.text: Use the formula: $n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)$.

blocks.answer: 80 people like either jollof rice or fried rice.

blocks.markdown: Now, let's consider a more complex scenario involving three sets. Such problems require careful analysis and filling regions from the inside out.

blocks.title: Exam Tip
blocks.text: When solving three-set problems, always start by filling the intersection of all three sets first, then move outwards to two-set intersections, and finally single sets.

points: Two-set problems use the formula $n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)$.
In three-set problems, fill regions starting from the intersection of all three sets.
